items.question: What must be established before deciding that the stomach is on the fetal left?
options: Fetal laterality, from the position of the fetus in the uterus
The cardiac axis
The heart rate
The position of the placenta
items.explanation: Fetal right and left are determined first, from the position of the fetus in utero; only then are stomach and heart confirmed on the left.

items.question: At which level is abdominal situs assessed?
options: The level of the standard abdominal circumference
The level of the bladder
The level of the kidneys
The level of the four-chamber view
items.explanation: Abdominal situs is assessed at the level of the standard abdominal circumference.

items.question: In normal situs, where do the great vessels lie in the upper-abdomen plane?
options: Descending aorta left of the spine; inferior vena cava right of the spine
Descending aorta right of the spine; inferior vena cava left of the spine
Both in front of the spine in the midline
Both to the left of the spine
items.explanation: Stomach on the left, descending aorta on the left and inferior vena cava on the right side of the spine.

items.question: Why does normal abdominal situs matter for the heart?
options: It is a surrogate for normal atrial situs
It proves the outflow tracts are normal
It shows the heart rate is regular
It rules out all heart disease
items.explanation: Normal abdominal situs stands in for normal atrial situs: right atrium to the right, left atrium to the left.

items.question: After working out fetal left and right, you find the stomach on the fetal right and the heart on the fetal left. What should you suspect?
options: A situs abnormality
A normal variant
A diaphragmatic hernia only
Nothing; only the heart's side matters
items.explanation: A situs abnormality should be suspected when the heart and/or the stomach are not on the left.

items.question: The heart is displaced to the right but the stomach is on the left. Which of these can displace the heart from its normal position?
options: Diaphragmatic hernia
An echogenic intracardiac focus
A thin rim of pericardial fluid
Occasional ectopic beats
items.explanation: Displacement can be caused by diaphragmatic hernia, a space-occupying lesion such as a congenital pulmonary airway malformation, or lung hypoplasia or agenesis.

items.question: The four-chamber view is poor because of fetal position. Can cardiac position and axis still be judged?
options: Yes: they can be evaluated even when the four-chamber view is not seen satisfactorily
No: they need a perfect four-chamber view
Only with colour Doppler
Only in the third trimester
items.explanation: Cardiac axis and position can be evaluated even when the four-chamber view itself is not seen satisfactorily.

items.question: An abnormal cardiac axis raises the risk of what in particular?
options: A cardiac malformation, especially of the outflow tracts
Benign ectopic beats
A normal variant of the third trimester
A technical artefact
items.explanation: An abnormal axis increases the risk of a cardiac malformation, especially of the outflow tracts, and may be associated with a chromosomal anomaly.
